Abel.note: A Hebrew name, indeclinable in Latin. The second son of Adam, whose offering of sheep was accepted where Cain's was not (Gen 4).

Abraham.note: A Hebrew name; Latin gives it the genitive Ábrahæ but declines the rest of the cases unevenly.

Agatha.note: A Greek name, “good”. The Sicilian martyr named in the Canon.

Agnes.note: A Greek name, “pure”; Latin ears heard agnus, lamb, in it, which is why she is shown with one.

Baptista.note: A 1st-declension noun, yet masculine — like “agrícola”, farmer; from Greek “baptistés” — one who immerses.

Christus.note: Greek Christós — “the anointed one” — rendering Hebrew Mashiach (Messiah).

Clemens.note: The name means “merciful”; the same word stands in the Canon as an adjective — clementíssime Pater.

Eva.note: The name of the first mother, Hebrew for the living one. The prayer calls us her banished children.

Felicitas.note: The name is an ordinary Latin noun — happiness, good fortune.

Iacobus.note: From Hebrew Yaakov. The Canon names him twice: they are two different apostles.

Iesus.note: The Greek form of Hebrew Yeshua — “the Lord saves”; irregular declension (nominative Iesus, accusative Iesum, all other cases Iesu).

Ioseph.note: A Hebrew name, indeclinable. It entered the Canon only in 1962: the one change St John XXIII made to this text.

Lucia.note: The name comes from lux — light.

Matthias.note: The apostle chosen by lot in place of Judas (Acts 1). A different name from Matthew, though both grow from the same Hebrew root.

Melchisedech.note: A Hebrew name, indeclinable. The king of Salem who brought out bread and wine (Gen 14); Hebrews makes him the figure of Christ's priesthood.

Michael.note: From Hebrew Mika'el — “Who is like God?”.

Perpetua.note: The name is a Latin adjective — “continual”. The Carthaginian martyr, whose prison diary survives.

Pilatus.note: A Roman cognomen; Pilate governed Judea for Rome under the emperor Tiberius.

Pontius.note: A Roman clan name (nomen); Pilátus was the cognomen that went with it.

Stephanus.note: A Greek name, “crown”; the first martyr (Acts 7).

Xystus.note: The Greek spelling of the name Latin later settled as Sixtus.

ab.note: “a” before consonants; “ab” before vowels and h (and at times before consonants too: ab hómine).

absolutio.note: A noun from absólvere — to loose, to set free; absolution looses from guilt.

ac.note: A variant of “atque” used before consonants; it binds more closely than et.

acceptus.note: A participle of accípere hardened into an adjective. The phrase accépta habére — to hold as received — is legal language, not devotional.

adhaereo.note: Ad and hǽreo, to stick to something; it governs the dative.

adiutorium.note: A noun from adjuváre — to help.

adiuvo.note: Ad and juvo, to help toward something; the same stem as adjutórium.

adscribo.note: Literally to write in beside — to enter on a register. The Canon asks that the offering be entered on the list of the accepted.

aduno.note: A late-Latin compound of ad and unus; classical Latin does not have it.

advocata.note: The feminine of advocátus — one called to another's side (ad and voco) to stand by the accused.

aestimator.note: From æstimáre, to put a price on; a word from accounts and courts.

aeternus.note: Contracted from ævitérnus, from ævum — an age, a long span of time.

affligo.note: Literally to dash against the ground (ad + fligo); hence to afflict.

agnus.note: “Ecce Agnus Dei” (Jn 1:29) — the Baptist's words at the Jordan; hence the Lamb as a liturgical name of Christ.

ago.note: A verb of very broad meaning; in the liturgy most often in the idiom “grátias ágere” — to give thanks.

alius.note: Declines like a pronoun: genitive alíus, dative álii — not like the -us, -a, -um adjectives.

alleluia.note: Hebrew hallelu-Yah, praise Yah(weh), taken into Latin through Greek and never declined. From Septuagesima until the Easter Vigil the liturgy does not say it once.

altare.note: Classical Latin calls an altar ara; altáre (more often the plural altária) is the word of Scripture and the liturgy.

altus.note: The superlative “Altíssimus” — the Most High — is a constant scriptural title of God.

amen.note: A Hebrew word taken into Latin unchanged — indeclinable; the solemn seal of a prayer.

angelus.note: Greek ángelos means simply “messenger”; Latin took the word over untranslated.

anima.note: The same root as ánimus (mind, spirit); ánima is the breath that gives life.

animus.note: Ánimus is the acting spirit — will and intent; ánima is the soul as the breath of life.

antistes.note: Literally one who stands before — in pagan Latin the priest of a temple, in Christian Latin the bishop.

apostolicus.note: The adjective of apóstolus (apostle) — coming from the Apostles, belonging to them.

ascendo.note: A compound of ad (toward) + scándere (to climb) — the exact opposite of descéndere.

atque.note: Stronger than et: it binds what it lists into one pair.

audeo.note: A semi-deponent: the present system is ordinary and active, the perfect passive in form and active in meaning (ausus sum, I dared).

aufero.note: A compound of ab + fero — to carry off; it inflects irregularly, like fero. Its supine ablátum gave the ablative case its name.

autem.note: It never stands first in its sentence — always after the first word.

aveo.note: A defective verb: in practice almost only the imperatives “ave”, “avéte”, used as a greeting.

baptisma.note: A Greek loanword (báptisma — an immersion), neuter, declined in the 3rd declension: genitive baptísmatis.

benedico.note: A compound of bene (well) + dícere (to say) — to bless is literally “to speak well”.

benedictus.note: From “bene dícere” — to speak well (of someone).

benignus.note: A compound of bonus and the root of gigno — well-born, and so kindly by nature.

caelum.note: The plural “cæli” is masculine; biblical Latin often speaks of heaven in the plural, after the Hebrew idiom.

capio.note: One of the basic Latin verbs; it belongs to the third conjugation in its -io pattern. Accípere, percípere and súscipere are all built on it.

caro.note: In Scripture it means the whole man in his weakness and mortality, not the body as against the soul.

catholicus.note: From Greek katholikós — universal, taken as a whole.

cenatus.note: From ceno, to dine. In the phrase cenátum est there is no subject: when supper was over.

circumsto.note: Its participle circumstántes is the Church Latin word for the congregation.

cithara.note: The Greek κιθάρα; in the psalms a stringed instrument sung to.

clamor.note: A noun from clamáre — to cry out; in the psalms the cry is prayer.

clementia.note: The virtue of a ruler who could punish and does not.

coaduno.note: A late-Latin verb from co- and unus: to bring many to one. Classical Latin does not have it.

cognosco.note: A compound of gnósco, to come to know — the same root as Greek gnósis.

commixtio.note: From commiscére, to mix together; a late-Latin noun, used once in the Roman liturgy.

communico.note: From commúnis, common. In Church Latin it means to stand in union with someone, and from it comes communion.

comprehendo.note: Literally to seize together — hence both taking hold with the hand and grasping with the mind.

concelebro.note: A compound of cum and celebráre. Here it is said of the choirs of angels, not of priests: the modern sense of concelebration is a much later use.

condemnatio.note: From condemnáre, to sentence; in a Roman court the verdict itself, not the trial.

condo.note: The verb for founding cities and establishing laws; hence “ab Urbe cóndita”.

confessio.note: A confession may be of guilt or of faith and praise; in the Preface it is the second.

confiteor.note: In church Latin also “to praise”: Confitémini Dómino.

conglorifico.note: A rare compound of cum (together) + glorificáre; it calques a Greek verb built with syn- (together with).

consecratio.note: From consecráre, to make over to a god; pagan Latin used it of an emperor's enrolment among the gods.

consors.note: Con-sors: one who shares another's lot (sors).

consortium.note: From cum and sors, lot: consórtes are those to whom the same lot has fallen.

conspectus.note: “In conspéctu” means before the face of, in the presence of.

consubstantialis.note: A theological coinage rendering Greek homooúsios — of the same substance; formed from cum + substántia.

contritus.note: The participle of contérere — to grind to powder.

conturbo.note: A compound of cum + turbáre — to stir up thoroughly.

conversio.note: From convérto, to turn round. A conversion in Latin is the turning of a whole person, not a change of mind.

converto.note: A compound of cum + vértere — to turn; the passive often means to turn oneself toward someone.

cooperor.note: Deponent: passive in form, active in meaning. Con- and óperor, to work alongside.

credo.note: Classically with the dative of the person (credo tibi — I believe you); the profession of faith says “credo in” with the accusative — I believe in. The whole Symbol of faith is named the Credo after its first word.

crucifigo.note: A running-together of cruci fígere — to fasten to a cross (crux, crucis + fígere).

cultor.note: From cólere, which means both to till the soil and to worship; one word for both, and the root of culture and cult.

datum.note: The participle of do used as a noun. The pair dona ac data — gifts and grants — comes from the language of Roman offerings.

de.note: Close to ex, but ex points to coming out from inside, de to separation from something or motion downward.

defunctus.note: From defúngi — to discharge, to have done with; the dead have finished with life.

descendo.note: A compound of de (down) + scándere (to climb).

detrudo.note: A compound of de and trudo, to push: to push so that a thing falls.

deus.note: Classical Latin avoided a vocative of “deus”; Church Latin simply calls “Deus”.

devotio.note: Originally the solemn dedication of oneself to a god, death included; Christian Latin softened it to dedication and piety.

dextera.note: Understand “(manus) déxtera” — the right hand; “at the right hand” is Scripture's place of honor.

diabolus.note: From Greek diábolos, one who throws accusations across; Latin took the word untranslated.

dies.note: One of the few 5th-declension nouns; usually masculine, feminine especially of an appointed day.

dignor.note: A deponent (passive form, active meaning) from dignus — worthy; dignéris is a courteous petition: be pleased to.

dilectus.note: A participle of díligo, to love by choice rather than by feeling; the word used of the beloved Son at the Baptism.

diligo.note: Love by choice — literally to pick out from among; amáre speaks of feeling.

directus.note: Its neuter diréctum serves as a noun: the straight way.

discerno.note: A compound of dis + cérnere — to separate, to sift apart.

discipulus.note: From díscere, to learn; a disciple is a learner, not a follower.

dominatio.note: In the Preface this is the name of one of the choirs of angels, drawn from Col 1:16 and Eph 1:21.

domus.note: It declines mostly in the 4th declension but keeps some 2nd declension forms — hence the wavering in dictionaries.

dono.note: From “donum”, a gift. It gives a thing (accusative) to a person (dative); classical Latin can also reverse the pattern and present a person (accusative) with something (ablative).

dormio.note: The Canon says of the dead that they sleep; the same idea named the cemetery, Greek for a sleeping-place.

dulcedo.note: The noun of dulcis; the ending -edo makes nouns of quality, as in altitúdo.

ecce.note: A pointing interjection; it takes the nominative, so the noun after it is not an object.

ecclesia.note: From Greek ekklesía — an assembly of those called out; Christian Latin uses it both of the community and of the building.

efficio.note: A compound of ex and fácio: to work a thing out, to carry it through.

eia.note: An interjection of urging. Its i is vocalic and its ei a diphthong — hence two syllables and no accent.

eleison.note: Greek ἐλέησον, the imperative of ἐλεέω “to have mercy”. In Greek it is an aorist: mercy asked for as a single act. Like Kýrie, the word has no entry of its own in the Latin dictionaries.

enim.note: Never stands first in its clause: Latin slips it into second place.

eo.note: An irregular verb whose stem can shrink to a single letter (it — he goes); the plural imperative is ite.

eripio.note: A compound of ex and rápio — to tear away by force; stronger than to free.

eruo.note: Literally to dig out; hence to snatch someone from danger.

evangelium.note: From Greek euangélion, good tidings; Latin took the word over untranslated.

ex.note: Before a vowel always “ex”; before a consonant both “e” and “ex” occur (ex María Vírgine).

exaltatio.note: From exálto, to raise high — ex- intensifying altus, high.

exaudio.note: An intensified audíre — not merely to hear but to grant what is heard.

excelsus.note: “In excélsis” — in the highest, that is, in the heavens; the plural follows the Hebrew idiom of the psalms.

exilium.note: From ex and solum, the soil: the state of one who is off his own ground.

exspecto.note: A compound of ex + spectáre (to look) — to look out for; some editions print the simplified spelling “expécto”.

exsul.note: The noun of the same root as exílium.

exsultatio.note: From exsultáre, to leap up; a joy that cannot keep still.

facio.note: In the present system its passive is supplied by fio (to become); the perfect passive is factus sum.

factor.note: A noun from fácere (to make) — “the one who makes”; in the Creed a title of God as maker of all.

familia.note: In Latin it means first the whole household, servants included, and only later the family in our sense; the Canon uses it of the whole Church.

fidelis.note: In the plural it stands as a noun: fidéles, the faithful.

fides.note: One word for faith and for faithfulness: in Latin they are the same thing seen from two sides.

finis.note: In the plural fines means boundaries, and hence the territory they enclose.

fio.note: Irregular; serves as the passive of “fácere”, to do or make.

fortitudo.note: From fortis — strong; in the psalms God's might, among the virtues fortitude.

futurus.note: Originally the future participle of sum; Latin uses it as a plain adjective too, and in the neuter plural for “things to come”.

gaudeo.note: A semi-deponent: active in form in the present tenses, passive in the perfect — gavísus sum, I rejoiced. English joy and enjoy descend from its noun gaudium by way of French.

genetrix.note: The feminine agent noun of gigno, to beget; the same root as génitus. The spellings genetrix and genitrix run side by side in the books.

gens.note: The same root as gígnere — to beget; a gens is those sprung from one stock.

gigno.note: The present stem is reduplicated (gi-gn-o) beside the root gen- seen in génui and génitum.

habito.note: A frequentative of hábeo, to have: to dwell is to keep on having, to hold a place.

hic.note: The demonstrative of what is near the speaker; not to be confused with the adverb hic — here.

hic_adverbium.note: The adverb of place; not the demonstrative hic, hæc, hoc — this.

hosanna.note: A Hebrew cry, “save, we pray”, from Ps 117:25; on the lips of the crowd greeting Christ (Mt 21:9) it is already pure acclamation — which is why Latin leaves it untranslated. Indeclinable.

hostia.note: In classical Latin a sacrificial animal — not bread; the eucharistic sense is later.

humilitas.note: From húmus — the ground; lowliness is being low to the earth.

idem.note: It is the pronoun is with the ending -dem; before d the m turns to n (eúndem).

igitur.note: Usually not first in its clause; in the Canon it stands second, after Te and after Hanc.

ille.note: The demonstrative of what is farther off; in Christian Latin often simply he. The Romance definite articles (il, le, el) descend from it.

illibatus.note: From libáre, to take a portion from an offering; illibátus is what nothing has been taken from.

immaculatus.note: From mácula — a stain; literally without a spot.

impero.note: Governs the dative: one commands TO someone, not someone.

impius.note: The opposite of pius — one who renders what is due to God and to parents.

incarno.note: A verb of Christian Latin, formed from caro, carnis (flesh).

incedo.note: A compound of in + cédere — to step forward; it names a manner of walking, not motion in general.

indulgentia.note: In the Church's language it became a technical term: an indulgence, the remission of temporal punishment.

indulgeo.note: It governs the dative of the person: indulgére alicui — to be gracious to someone.

inferi.note: Always plural: literally those below. Ab ínferis means from among the dead, not from hell.

infernus.note: From inférus, lower: the place set lower than everything else.

inhaereo.note: In and hǽreo, to stick to; used both of things glued and of a man faithful to a cause. It governs the dative.

inimicus.note: The negation of amícus (friend): in- + amícus.

iniquitas.note: From iníquus; at the bottom of it lies the lack of æquus — of what is even and fair.

iniquus.note: The negation of æquus (even, fair): in- + æquus.

initium.note: The noun of íneo, to go in: that which is entered first.

innocens.note: In-nocens: one who does no harm.

insidiae.note: A noun only in the plural; literally a sitting in hiding (in and sédeo).

institutio.note: From instítuere, to set up: in liturgical Latin the setting-up of a rite by Christ himself.

intercedo.note: Inter-cédere: to stand between the one asking and the one asked.

intro.note: From intra, within. Not to be confused with the adverb intro, inwards, spelt the same.

introeo.note: A compound of intro (inwards) + ire (to go); it inflects irregularly, like ire. Its supine gives intróitus — an entrance, and hence the name of the entrance chant.

invisibilis.note: The negation of visíbilis by the prefix in-.

invoco.note: In and voco, to call toward; invocáre nomen Dómini is a fixed scriptural phrase.

ipse.note: The intensive pronoun: it presses on the person or thing spoken of.

is.note: The most colourless demonstrative: it points without stressing nearness or distance.

iste.note: It points at what is near the person addressed, or at hand where the speaker stands.

iudicium.note: From judex, a judge; it covers both the trial and the power of judging.

iudico.note: Formed from júdex (judge), itself from jus, juris (law) + dícere (to speak) — the one who declares the law.

iuventus.note: From júvenis — young; the collective noun also means the young as a body.

kyrie.note: Greek κύριε, the vocative of κύριος “lord”. No Latin dictionary heads the bare word — Latin took the whole formula instead: Niermeyer heads kyrie-eleison as a noun for the chant itself, and Du Cange has kyrieles for the litany and the verb kyrieleisare, “to sing Kyrie eleison”.

lacryma.note: Lacryma and lacrima are one word; the y came in when the ending was felt to be Greek.

laetifico.note: A compound of lætus (glad) + fácere — to make glad.

laetor.note: A deponent (passive form, active meaning) from lætus — glad.

largitor.note: From largíri, to give lavishly; in secular Latin often said of political largesse.

liber.note: Not the noun liber, libri, a book, nor líberi, liberórum, children — literally “the free ones” as against the household's slaves.

libertas.note: From liber, free — the condition of one who is not a slave.

loquor.note: It stresses speaking as an activity; dícere stresses what is said.

luceo.note: The same root as lux. Intransitive: the light shines of itself, it does not shine on something.

lumen.note: The same root as lux; lumen is usually light as it is seen — brightness, or a lamp.

lux.note: Lux is light itself; lumen is the light a thing gives off (compare lumen de lúmine in the Credo).

macula.note: First a mark on cloth or skin, only afterwards a moral stain; immaculátus, spotless, is its negative.

malignus.note: A compound of malus and gigno: one who breeds evil. Its opposite is benígnus.

mandatum.note: The passive participle of mandáre used as a noun: the thing entrusted. The Maundy of Holy Thursday takes its name from this word.

manduco.note: A colloquial word — to chew, not the polite édere; biblical Latin chose it, and the Romance languages kept it (French manger).

martyr.note: Greek mártys means simply witness; Latin took the word over untranslated, and the sense of one who died for the faith is the Church's addition.

medela.note: From médeor, to heal; the same stem as medicus and medicína.

memini.note: A defective verb: it has only perfect forms, but a present sense. Its imperative meménto is a future imperative — the only imperative it possesses.

memor.note: It governs the genitive: mindful of a thing, never mindful a thing.

mereo.note: With an infinitive in liturgical Latin it usually means to be granted something rather than to have earned it: the soldier's sense of wages is the classical one, the sense of gift the Church's.

mereor.note: A deponent (passive form, active meaning); mereámur — that we may be counted worthy.

meritum.note: The noun of meréri — to deserve.

mirabilis.note: Its neuter plural stands as a noun: mirabília, wonders, the things worth wondering at.

mirabiliter.note: Its comparative is mirabílius, which is spelt the same as the neuter of the adjective.

miseratio.note: Not the feeling of pity but its exercise: in the plural, particular acts of mercy.

misereor.note: In liturgical formulas with the dative (miserére nobis); classically and in the psalms with the genitive (miserére mei).

misericordia.note: A compound of míserum cor — a heart for the wretched; the same build as miséricors.

misericors.note: A compound of miser (wretched) + cor (heart): having a heart for the wretched.

miseror.note: A deponent (passive form, active meaning). Its participle miseránte is active in form, as every deponent's present participle is.

missa.note: A late Latin noun built on missus (sent away). From this one word the whole liturgy took its name — missa, Mass, Messe, msza.

mitto.note: From its participle missus comes missa, the name of the Mass.

moneo.note: From the same root as mens and memini: to make someone mindful.

mortuus.note: The perfect participle of mórior (to die), used both as an adjective and as a noun: mórtui, the dead.

munio.note: From mœnia, city walls; to muníre is to wall something round.

nascor.note: From the participle natus come natúra and natívitas (nativity).

nec.note: A shortened neque. The pair nec non does not mean nor not: two negatives cancel, and it reads as an emphatic and also.

negligentia.note: The fault of omission — what was left undone.

neque.note: The same word as nec in its full shape.

nihil.note: Indeclinable. From ne and hilum, the speck on a bean — not even that much.

non.note: It negates a single word or a whole clause; prohibitions and negative petitions use ne instead.

numquam.note: Ne and umquam, not ever; the negation is built into the word.

o.note: The interjection of the vocative: it is not translated on its own but strengthens an address.

oblatio.note: The noun of offérre — the thing carried up before God.

obsequium.note: From ob and sequor — to follow after; hence the service shown to the one followed.

offensio.note: A fault against someone, not the bad deed in itself.

offero.note: A compound of ob- and fero, and the source of the name of the offertory. It declines irregularly, like fero.

ops.note: Classical Latin does not use the nominative singular; the living forms are opem, opis, ope. The plural opes means “wealth”.

oratio.note: The noun of oráre; in classical Latin a speech, in Christian Latin chiefly a prayer.

orbis.note: Orbis terrárum, the circle of the lands, is the Roman name for the whole known world.

oro.note: The call “Orémus” — let us pray — is the same verb.

orthodoxus.note: From Greek orthós, straight, and dóxa, opinion. In the Canon it is not the name of a communion but a description of those who hold the Church's faith.

os.note: Not to be confused with os, ossis, a bone; the two match in the nominative but differ in stem. Oratio and osculum come from this one.

ostendo.note: A compound of obs (ob) + téndere — to stretch out before someone.

papa.note: Greek páppas, daddy; in the East a title for any priest, in the West reserved to the bishop of Rome from the fifth century.

particeps.note: Pars-cápere: one who takes a part.

participatio.note: From pártem cápere, to take a part; not presence but a share received.

patior.note: From the participle passus comes pássio — suffering, the Passion.

patriarcha.note: A Greek noun in -a; Latin declines it like the feminine 1st declension while its gender stays masculine.

peccatum.note: The noun of pecco (to sin) — the deed, not the disposition.

per.note: It expresses mediation — hence the standing close of the orations, “per Christum Dóminum nostrum”.

perceptio.note: From percípere, to take fully; in liturgical Latin the settled word for receiving Communion.

percipio.note: Per and cápio, to take through to the end; hence both “obtain” and “understand”.

perditio.note: The noun of perdo, to destroy utterly.

senses: to bring all the way to
perduco.note: A compound of per + dúcere — to lead right to the end.

perfero.note: A compound of per and fero, and as irregular: its principal parts come from three different roots.

perhibeo.note: A compound of per and hábeo. In biblical Latin almost only in the phrase testimónium perhibére, to bear witness.

permitto.note: Per and mitto, to let through, to let go; hence both “allow” and “leave a matter in someone's hands”.

perpetuus.note: From pétere, to make for: what runs on unbroken to the end. Slightly different from ætérnus, which speaks of having no limit.

perturbatio.note: From perturbáre, to throw into confusion; it covers outward disorder and inward agitation alike.

pervagor.note: A deponent (passive form, active meaning). A compound of per and vagor — to wander the length of a thing.

pietas.note: For a Roman, the duty owed to parents, gods and country — hence pius Æneas. Said of God it means His faithfulness toward us.

pius.note: Roman píetas is faithfulness towards the gods, one's parents and one's country; the adjective carries all of it.

placatus.note: A participle of placáre hardened into an adjective: not open to appeasement but already appeased.

placeo.note: It governs the dative of the person: to be pleasing to someone.

plebs.note: At Rome the order set against the patricians; in Church Latin simply the people.

senses: full of (with the ablative or genitive)

populus.note: A people taken as one body, not a crowd of persons; in Roman law, the citizens together.

porto.note: An everyday word for carrying a load; the same root carries transport and export. It has nothing to do with porta, a gate.

potestas.note: In the Preface the name of a choir of angels, beside the Dominations; both come from Col 1:16.

poto.note: The plain everyday word for drinking; pótio, a draught, and potátor, a drinker, come from it.

praeceptum.note: Properly the passive participle of præcípere, to take beforehand, to enjoin: the thing enjoined.

praeclarus.note: Literally very bright; the præ- here intensifies rather than meaning before.

praelium.note: Prælium and proelium are one word; the liturgical books print prælium.

praesens.note: Originally the active participle of præesse, to be at hand; hence both “present in place” and “present in time”.

praesidium.note: From præsídeo, to sit in front of a thing and guard it.

praesumo.note: Præ and sumo, to take in advance or without leave; hence both “assume in advance” and “dare”.

praeteritus.note: Originally the passive participle of præteríre, to go past; Latin settled it as an adjective in its own right, and the dictionaries head it as one.

prex.note: In classical Latin almost always plural — preces; the singular is rare.

pridie.note: A word from the Roman calendar: prídie Kaléndas, the day before the first of the month.

primus.note: The phrase in primis (first of all) has set as a whole and no longer marks a gender.

princeps.note: A compound of primus and cápio: the one who takes first place.

senses: to proceed, to come forth from
procedo.note: A compound of pro (forward) + cédere (to go); in trinitarian language it is the verb for one divine Person's origin from another.

promissio.note: The noun of promítto, to send forth and so to promise — from the same mitto as missa.

propheta.note: A 1st-declension noun, yet masculine — like “agrícola”, farmer; from Greek “prophétes” — one who speaks for another.

propitiabilis.note: A late and rare word built on propitius: that through which propitiation is made.

propitius.note: A word from Roman sacrifice: a propítium god is one whose offering has been received.

proprius.note: Hence the proprium — the parts of the Mass proper to the day, as against the unchanging ordinarium.

prosum.note: A compound of sum, irregular, inserting d before a vowel (prodest, prodésse). It governs the dative.

protectio.note: From tégere, to roof over; a protéctio is a roof held out above someone.

provenio.note: Pro and vénio, to come forward; it speaks of the result something comes out to, good or bad.

puer.note: It means both boy and servant, as Greek país does. Of Abel the Canon says púeri tui — thy servant.

quaeso.note: A defective verb: chiefly quæso and quǽsumus survive, dropped into a request as English drops in “please”. It is an older form of the verb quærere — to seek, to ask for.

quam.note: After prídie (the day before) Latin puts quam — the day earlier than — where English says before.

quare.note: A fusion of qua re — for what cause.

quasi.note: A fusion of quam and si, as if. It does not equate: it states a likeness.

quia.note: Classical Latin mostly “because”; church Latin, following the Greek, also uses “quia” for “that” after verbs of saying and confessing.

quis.note: The interrogative pronoun; the indefinite (someone, something) has the same forms and is told apart by its place in the sentence, especially after si, nisi, ne and num.

quoque.note: It follows the word it belongs to, never precedes it.

quotidianus.note: In the Lord's Prayer it renders the Greek “epioúsios”, a word almost unattested elsewhere.

quotquot.note: Indeclinable: the form marks neither case nor gender nor number.

rationabilis.note: The Canon follows Rom 12:1: rationábile obséquium, a reasonable service — that is, spiritual rather than animal sacrifice.

ratus.note: A legal term: a ratus agreement is one that holds good. Ratification comes from it.

recipio.note: A compound of re and cápio: to take to oneself what comes.

reddo.note: Vota réddere is a technical phrase: to discharge a vow made to a god, to pay what was promised.

redemptio.note: From émere, to buy; a redémptio is the buying back of a slave or a captive for a price.

redimo.note: Red-émere: to buy back, to ransom a captive.

reficio.note: Re- and fácio, to make again; used of a meal that sets a tired traveller on his feet.

refrigerium.note: Literally a cooling. In early Christian tomb inscriptions it is the ordinary word for the state of the departed, and Roman families held a graveside meal called a refrigérium.

refugium.note: The noun of refúgio, to flee for help. It does not name the flight but the place fled to.

relinquo.note: Re- and linquo, to leave behind; the same stem as relíquiæ, the things left over.

reliquiae.note: A noun found only in the plural; from relínquere — to leave behind.

remaneo.note: Re- and máneo, to stay back, to be left over.

remedium.note: Re- and médeor, to heal back; the same stem as medéla and medicína.

senses: release from a debt or penalty
remissio.note: A noun from remíttere — to send back, to let go; the remission of sins is the letting go of them.

repello.note: A compound of re + péllere — to push away.

resurgo.note: A compound of re- (again) + súrgere (to rise).

resurrectio.note: The noun of resúrgere, to rise again.

retribuo.note: Re- and tríbuo, to allot back; the one word serves both for the gift given and for the gift returned.

sabaoth.note: A Hebrew word taken into Latin unchanged and never declined; a plural, “armies” — the armies of heaven. The Vulgate translates it at Is 6:3 (“Deus exercítuum”); the liturgical books keep the Hebrew.

sacerdos.note: From sacra dare, to offer holy things. A different word from presbýter, which gave English priest.

sacramentum.note: For a Roman, a soldier's oath and a pledge deposited in a temple; Christian Latin took the word over to render the Greek mystérion.

sacratus.note: The past participle of sacro, to consecrate. Its superlative, sacratíssimus, is the Church's word for what is most holy.

sacrificium.note: Sacrum fácere — to make holy; the sacrifice as an act, not as the gift.

sacrosanctus.note: A Roman legal term: a sacrosánctus person was one who could not be harmed without incurring a curse — the tribune of the plebs was.

saeculum.note: “In sǽcula sæculórum” — a Hebrew intensifying idiom: unto the ages of ages, world without end.

salus.note: In classical Latin chiefly health and safety; in Christian Latin salvation comes to the fore.

salutare.note: The adjective salutáris (saving) used as a noun. It is the word Simeon uses of the Child in the Nunc dimíttis (Lk 2:30).

salutaris.note: The same word used as a noun gives salutáre — salvation.

salveo.note: In practice only in the imperative: salve and salvéte are the Roman greeting — be well.

salvus.note: The same stem as salus and salvátor; first “whole, untouched”, only afterwards “saved”.

sanctificator.note: A noun in -tor names the doer of an action: the one who sanctifies.

sanctifico.note: A compound of “sanctus” and “fácere” — to make holy.

sanctus.note: Often used as a noun: “Sancti”, the Saints.

sanguis.note: Its plural sánguines means shed blood in the psalter, hence “viri sánguinum”, men of blood.

sano.note: From sanus, healthy; used of bodies and of repairing what is broken alike.

satanas.note: From Hebrew through Greek: the adversary, the accuser. It declines like the Greek masculines of the 1st declension.

scelus.note: A heavier word than peccátum: not a fault but a deed that cries out.

scriptura.note: From scríbere (to write); in the plural Scriptúræ — the Scriptures.

secundum.note: The accusative of the adjective secúndus (following), itself from sequi (to follow) — literally “following along”.

securus.note: Se- (without) and cura (care): first “carefree”, only later “safe”.

sempiternus.note: From semper, always. Beside ætérnus it stresses going on without end rather than standing outside time.

separo.note: Se- (apart) and paro, to set aside on its own.

sepelio.note: The participle sepúltus departs from the infinitive sepelíre; from the same stem comes sepultúra, burial.

seraphim.note: A Hebrew plural (singular seraph) taken over undeclined; Latin treats it as a neuter plural. The root means to burn.

serenus.note: First said of a cloudless sky, and only then of a face.

servitus.note: Stronger than service: it is the condition of a slave. The Canon uses it of a service freely given to God.

sicuti.note: Sicut with an added -i; the same meaning, a more formal sound. The stress falls on the first syllable.

signum.note: Signum fídei, the sign of faith, has meant baptism since antiquity; that is how the Canon speaks of the baptized dead.

sine.note: Governs the ablative — the opposite of the preposition cum, which governs the same case.

socius.note: The adjective of sócius, a companion; sócia exsultatióne means in shared exultation.

spero.note: In the psalms with in and the ablative: speráre in Deo — to put one's hope in God.

sponsus.note: From spondére, to pledge solemnly; the bridegroom is the one pledged to.

senses: in the time of, under (a ruler)

sui.note: A reflexive pronoun with no nominative and no number: one form serves for one and for many.

summus.note: The superlative of súperus (upper); it has no positive degree of its own.

sumo.note: In liturgical Latin the standing word for receiving Communion.

supplex.note: From sub and plicáre, to bend down under; a posture of the body, not only a tone of voice.

surgo.note: Contracted from sub-régere, to lead upward. Without the re- of resúrgo it says only that someone rose.

sursum.note: A contraction of sub-vórsum, turned upward; an adverb of direction, not a preposition.

suspiro.note: A compound of sub and spiro: breath drawn from below.

suus.note: The reflexive possessive: it looks back to the subject of the sentence, unlike eius — his, of someone else.

tabernaculum.note: A diminutive of tabérna — a hut, a booth; in Scripture the tent of meeting.

tantum.note: A frozen neuter accusative of tantus used adverbially; the sense “only” comes from “just so much and no more”.

tectum.note: The passive participle of tego, to cover, used as a noun: the thing that covers. Latin commonly uses it for a house entire.

temporalis.note: From tempus, time; in Church Latin the standing opposite of ætérnus.

tenebrae.note: The noun exists only in the plural. From it the Tenebrae of Holy Week take their name.

testamentum.note: A Roman testamentum is a disposition made against one's death; biblical Latin used the word for the Hebrew covenant, and both senses sound in the words of consecration.

tollo.note: In the liturgy both senses at once: the Lamb “lifts” the world's sins onto himself and so “takes them away”.

totus.note: Its genitive is totíus and its dative toti — a pronominal declension, not the ordinary adjectival one.

tribuo.note: Originally to share out among the tribus, the Roman tribes; hence to allot.

tristis.note: A two-termination adjective: one form for masculine and feminine (tristis), another for neuter (triste).

tutamentum.note: From tueor, to watch over; a late and rare word, hardly met outside the liturgy.

una.note: The ablative of unus set hard as an adverb; una cum means together with.

unde.note: The interrogative whence used as an inferential connective: this being so, therefore.

unigenitus.note: A compound of unus (one) + génitus (begotten) — the only one begotten.

unus.note: It takes pronominal endings in the genitive (uníus) and the dative (uni).

ut.note: With the subjunctive it means so that; with the indicative, as.

uti.note: An older form of ut; spelt like the infinitive of utor (to use), but a different word.

vel.note: It allows both alternatives, unlike aut, which rules one of them out.

veneror.note: A deponent: passive in form, active in meaning. The same root as the name of Venus.

venia.note: Not the cancelling of a debt but a gracious leave; hence a venial sin — peccátum veniále, one readily pardoned.

venio.note: The base of many compounds: advénio (to come to), convénio (to come together), invénio (to find).

vester.note: The possessive of the second person plural. Its form vestri also serves as the genitive of the pronoun vos.

vir.note: Vir is a male; homo is a human being of either sex.

virtus.note: From vir, a man: first manliness, then any excellence, at last virtue. In the Preface it names a choir of angels.

viscus.note: Almost always plural, víscera. Literally the organs under the ribs; by transference, whatever is innermost in a person.

visibilis.note: From vidére (to see); the suffix -bilis makes adjectives of possibility — able to be seen.

vita.note: The same root as vivus (alive) and vívere (to live).

vivifico.note: A compound of vivus (alive) + fácere (to make) — to make alive.

vivus.note: Used as a noun: vivi, the living.

vos.note: Its genitive has two shapes: vestri (objective, as in misereátur vestri) and vestrum (partitive).

votum.note: From vovére, to vow; vota are also the offerings hung up when a prayer has been answered.

vultus.note: Vultus is the face as it looks out — the expression; fácies is the face as a shape.
